name: Peace-list activists with confirmed multi-day US custody
eligibility: Documented actual US custody beyond initial arrest processing, lasting multiple days, in a case connected with political or civil-disobedience activity.

prisoner.name: Ellen Thomas
prisoner.description: Ellen Thomas is an anti-nuclear activist associated with the White House Peace Vigil and Proposition One. She challenged restrictions on the vigil in Lafayette Park and served a jail sentence in the camping case she appealed with William Thomas.

cases.sentence: Served 30 days in the 1988 camping case arising from March 1987 vigil activity. Exact custody endpoints are unverified.

entries.coordinate_note: Approximate city point for the documented case location, not a prison address.
entries.research_limits: Only the court-confirmed 30-day case is created. Other 1988 custody episodes require separate case research; no approximate total is converted into exact dates.

prisoner.name: William Thomas Hallenback Jr.
prisoner.description: William Thomas, also known as Doubting Thomas, maintained a long-running anti-nuclear vigil opposite the White House beginning in 1981. He and Ellen Thomas contested the use of park camping rules against their protest and served jail sentences in the resulting case.

cases.sentence: Served 30 days in the 1988 camping case arising from March 1987 vigil activity. Exact custody endpoints are unverified.

prisoner.aka: William Doubting Thomas; William Thomas (White House Peace Vigil)

entries.coordinate_note: Approximate city point for the documented case location, not a prison address.
entries.research_limits: Distinct from existing St. William Thomas, the WWI conscientious objector. Full legal name avoids merging the two. Exact custody endpoints and other detention episodes not inferred.

prisoner.name: George Lakey
prisoner.description: George Lakey is a Quaker activist, writer and educator in nonviolent action. During the 1963 civil-rights campaign in Chester, Pennsylvania, he joined a City Hall sit-in and spent a week in jail. In his first-person account, the judge dismissed the case after finding that a police officer had invited him to sit down.

cases.charges: Charges arising from the Chester City Hall civil-rights sit-in; exact statutory count unverified.
cases.sentence: One week in jail before the case was dismissed in 1963, according to Lakey’s first-person account.
cases.convicted: No; case dismissed on entrapment grounds, according to Lakey.

entries.coordinate_note: Approximate city point for the documented case location, not a prison address.
entries.research_limits: Exact arrest/release dates, charge wording and birth month/day not established by the cited sources. One week is documented custody, not a sentence.

prisoner.name: Robert Ellsberg
prisoner.description: Robert Ellsberg is a writer and publisher who participated in the Catholic Worker movement. He joined the 1978 anti-nuclear railroad blockade at Rocky Flats, Colorado. His statement to the Jefferson County court described 16 days already spent in jail, including nine in solitary confinement.

cases.charges: Prosecution arising from the Rocky Flats railroad blockade; exact statutory counts unverified.
cases.sentence: At least 16 days in Jefferson County jail in Golden by May 27, 1978, including nine in solitary confinement. The statement does not establish the final sentence or release date.

entries.coordinate_note: Approximate city point for the documented case location, not a prison address.
entries.research_limits: Sixteen days is a lower bound as of the court statement, not a final term. No arithmetic-derived arrest date or release date. Birth year only.

prisoner.name: Lenni Brenner
prisoner.description: Lenni Brenner, known as Lenny Glaser during the Berkeley Free Speech Movement, was a civil-rights and antiwar activist. He spent 39 months in California prison following revocation of probation in a marijuana case. Brenner and fellow activist Michael Rossman attributed the severity of his treatment to intervention by university authorities over his campus political activity.

cases.charges: Revocation of probation in a marijuana-possession case following 1964 campus activism.
cases.sentence: 39 months served in California prison. The political role of university intervention was alleged by Brenner and Michael Rossman; exact custody endpoints remain unverified.

entries.coordinate_note: Approximate city point for the documented case location, not a prison address.
entries.research_limits: No exact release date imported from unsourced summaries. Distinct from Leon Glaser, the Russian-born Seattle deportation prisoner in 1931. Documented months retained without invented dates.

prisoner.name: Adam Kokesh
prisoner.description: Adam Kokesh is a Marine veteran and antiwar activist who later organized libertarian civil-disobedience actions. In 2013 he spent approximately four months in US custody following a firearm protest in Washington, DC. This detention concerned his Freedom Plaza shotgun demonstration and associated criminal proceedings, rather than an antiwar demonstration.

cases.charges: Carrying a rifle or shotgun, possessing an unregistered firearm, and unlawful ammunition possession after the July 4, 2013 Freedom Plaza protest.
cases.sentence: Approximately four months in custody in 2013 before release following a guilty plea in November. This is time held before sentencing, not a four-month sentence.
cases.convicted: Yes; guilty plea November 6, 2013. A separate marijuana charge was also resolved that day.

entries.coordinate_note: Approximate city point for the documented case location, not a prison address.
entries.research_limits: Custody was in Virginia and DC; marker denotes the protest location. Approximate duration is not stored as an exact month counter. Later sentencing and unrelated cases are not combined with this detention.

thomas-court.label: United States v. William Thomas / Ellen Thomas, 864 F.2d 188 (D.C. Cir. 1988)
thomas-court.supports: Both served 30-day camping sentences. Conduct March 22–29, 1987; trial memorandum February 5, 1988; affirmed December 30, 1988. These are not exact custody endpoints.
